reader_question: How large was the House majority’s seat advantage in each Congress?
grade_line: Documented: the House’s own record of party divisions
title: Republicans won five more House seats than Democrats in the 2024 election, the smallest lead in the first count for any Congress since 1951.
reading_guide: Each row is one Congress, oldest at the top, dated by the year it opened. An arrow points toward the party that won the majority in the election before it, and its length is the majority’s lead in seats as first counted.
measure_line: Seats held by the majority party minus seats held by the other major party, as first elected for each Congress, House of Representatives, 82nd to 119th Congress, 1951 to 2027. The chart starts with the 82nd Congress so it covers the 38 Congresses of the last 75 years.
notes: Democrats won the majority for 25 of the 38 Congresses and Republicans for 13. Control changed hands seven times.
The largest lead was 155 seats, for Democrats in the 89th Congress, which opened in 1965.

The counts are the House’s figures from the first election results for each Congress, so deaths, resignations, special elections and party switches after that are left out. On November 11, 2026, the Clerk of the House listed 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies.
Members of other parties, never more than two in these years, count in neither side’s seats.
alt: Arrows for each Congress from 1951 to 2025 show the House majority’s lead in seats as first elected, pointing left for Democratic majorities and right for Republican ones. Democratic leads ran as high as 155 seats in 1965, leads since 1995 have mostly been under 60 seats, and Republicans won the 119th Congress, which opened in 2025, by five seats, the smallest lead in the chart.

table.caption: House seats as first elected for each Congress, by party

chart_notes: Arrows point left for a Democratic majority and right for a Republican majority, all in one ink. Both sides share one scale, and the center line sits off center to give the longer Democratic leads room.
The party is named beside the figure at the first row, at each row where the majority changed sides and at the 119th Congress, which the title names, where the figure is set bold.
